data.title: Server-Side Request Forgery
data.summary:
The application retrieved resources from URLs supplied in the request, allowing
an attacker to direct those requests at internal systems otherwise unreachable
from outside the network.
data.description:
The application accepted a URL as input and issued a request to it from the
server. Because the destination was not restricted, an attacker could supply
addresses referring to systems within the internal network, to the server itself
via its loopback interface, or to cloud platform metadata services.

Requests issued this way originate from the application server and therefore
carry its network position and, in some cases, its credentials. Controls that
restrict access based on source address treat the request as internal and permit
it. Services intentionally bound to the loopback interface on the assumption that
they are unreachable become accessible.

The technique permits the internal network to be mapped by observing differences
in response time and content between addresses that are reachable and those that
are not. Where the application returns the content retrieved, data from internal
services is disclosed directly; where it does not, the difference in behaviour
still reveals the state of the target.

Validation based on the hostname supplied is often insufficient, as
redirects, alternative address encodings, and DNS records resolving to internal
addresses each defeat it.
data.impact:
An attacker could reach internal systems from outside the network using the
application server as a relay, enumerate internal infrastructure, and interact
with services that rely on network position for their protection. Where cloud
metadata services are reachable, this may disclose credentials granting access to
the wider hosting environment.
data.recommendation:
1. Where the set of destinations is known, validate the supplied value against an
   allowlist of permitted hosts and reject anything else. This is the only
   reliable control.

2. Where arbitrary destinations must be supported, resolve the hostname and
   verify that the resulting address is not within private, loopback, or
   link-local ranges, repeating the check after every redirect rather than only
   on the initial value.

3. Disable redirect following and restrict the permitted schemes to HTTP and
   HTTPS, preventing the use of alternative protocol handlers.

4. Issue outbound requests through a dedicated egress proxy with its own
   allowlist, so that network controls enforce the restriction independently of
   the application.

5. Require authentication on internal services rather than relying on network
   position, and enforce the use of the instance metadata service version that
   requires a session token where the application is cloud hosted.

6. Return a generic response to the client rather than the content retrieved,
   where the business function permits.
